Plotting the improvement opportunities on the matrix allows the client to visualize and understand their key drivers for prioritization.

There are four main areas of this complexity chart:

  • Prioritize, Consider, Extra effort and Caution. By evaluating client initiatives on complexity and benefit, the chart allows the project team to classify initiatives into one of the four main categories. For example, an initiative that is of low complexity and high impact is considered a priority.
  • Proceed now, Long Term, Implement and Hold. By evaluating client projects on complexity and benefit, the chart allows the project team to classify the projects into one of the four main categories. For example, an initiative that is of high Ease of Implementation and high Benefit is considered a Quick Hit.

Prioritized improvement portfolios contain the ordered listing of improvement opportunities needed to move an organization to the future state. The improvement opportunities are ranked on an agreed upon set of criteria, such as:

  • Value impact (i.e. degree of change)
  • Difficulty of Implementation
  • Speed of benefit realization (i.e. pace of change)
  • Risk vs reward / benefit

Each opportunity may also contain other information such as:

  • Project sponsors and structure
  • Resources needed (both internal and external)
  • Timing estimates
  • Benefits realization information and metrics
  • Any potential impacts to the organization as a result of the implementation
  • Linkage and traceability to gaps, observations, root causes, pain points
  • Dependecies
  • Risks
  • Constraints
  • Assumptions

As an improvement portfolio is refined during the course of a project and develops into a deliverable that will be presented, other contextual information may be added in, such as background and scope, references back to a future state vision, guiding principles, and a summary of project activities to date.
To present prioritized improvement opportunities in a manner that allows for easy identification that highlights the expected benefits in relation to the anticipated complexity .
